title: Against idleness
paragraphs: The Emperor Vespasian, when he was dying of the disease that killed him, did not for a moment stop asking about the state of the empire, and even from his bed kept dispatching a great many affairs of consequence. When his physician scolded him for this as harmful to his health, he replied: "An emperor must die standing." A fine line, in my opinion, and worthy of a great prince. The Emperor Hadrian later used the same words, and kings should often be reminded of them, so they understand that the great office of command over so many men is not a leisurely employment. There is nothing that can more justly disgust a subject and make him unwilling to expose himself to hardship and danger for his prince than seeing the prince meanwhile devoted to ease and trivial amusement, anxious for the safety of his own person while neglecting that of his people.

Anyone who wants to argue that it is better for a prince to conduct his wars through others rather than in his own person will easily find examples from fortune of lieutenants who have brought great enterprises to a happy end, and others whose master's presence did more harm than good. But no virtuous and valiant prince can stomach so dishonourable a counsel. Under the pretext of preserving his head for the happiness of his kingdom, like the statue of a saint, they degrade him and pronounce him incapable of the office he holds, which is military through and through. I know one prince who would rather be beaten than sleep while another fights for him, and who never hears without a touch of jealousy of any brave deed done by his own officers in his absence. And Suleiman I said, with very good reason in my view, that victories obtained without the master are never complete. He might have said more — that the master should blush with shame to claim any share of the honour, having contributed nothing to the work but his voice and his thought. Not even those, considering that in such work the only direction and command that earn honour are the ones given on the spot, in the heat of action. No pilot does his job standing still. The princes of the Ottoman house, the foremost in the world for military fortune, have warmly embraced this view, and Bajazet II, along with his son, who broke with it and spent their time on learning and other retired pursuits, struck heavy blows against their empire. Murad III, who now reigns, is following their example and beginning to feel the same effect. Was it not Edward III of England who said this of our Charles V: "There has never been a king who put on his armour so seldom, and yet never a king who gave me so much trouble." He had reason to find it strange, as an effect of chance more than reason. And let those who want to count the kings of Castile and Portugal among the warlike and magnanimous conquerors look for someone other than me to agree — because, from twelve hundred leagues away in their idle quarters, by the conduct of their captains, they made themselves masters of both Indies, of which it remains to be seen whether they would even have had the courage to go and enjoy them in person.

The Emperor Julian went still further, saying that a philosopher and a brave man ought not even to breathe — that is, not to grant the body any more than what cannot be refused, keeping the soul and body always intent and busy on honourable, great, and virtuous things. He was ashamed if anyone in public saw him spit or sweat — something also reported of the young men of Lacedaemon, and which Xenophon says of the Persians — because he believed that exercise, continual labour, and sobriety should have dried up all such surplus. What Seneca says fits here too: that the ancient Romans kept their young men always on their feet and taught them nothing they were to learn sitting down.

It is a generous wish to want to die usefully and like a man, but the outcome lies less in our resolution than in our luck. A thousand have set out in battle either to win or die, and have failed at both, wounds and imprisonment cutting across their plan and forcing them to live on against their will. There are diseases that overthrow even our wishes and our knowledge. Fortune was not bound to back up the vanity of the Roman legions, who swore by oath either to win or to die:
"Victor, Marce Fabi, revertar ex acie: si fallo, Jovem patrem, Gradivumque Martem aliosque iratos invoco deos."
["I will return, Marcus Fabius, a conqueror, from the fight: and if I fail, I invoke Father Jove, Mars Gradivus, and the other angry gods." — Livy, ii. 45.]

The Portuguese say that at one place during their conquest of the Indies, they met soldiers who had bound themselves by horrible curses to make no other deal but either to be killed or to remain victorious, and had shaved their heads and beards in token of this vow. There is little point in throwing ourselves forward and being obstinate: it seems as if blows avoid those who present themselves too eagerly, and refuse to fall on those who too willingly invite them, defeating their purpose. Some, after trying everything, unable for all their efforts to obtain the favour of dying by the enemy's hand, have been forced, to make good their resolution of either bringing home victory or losing their lives, to kill themselves in the very heat of the battle. There are other examples, but here is one: Philistus, general of the naval forces of the younger Dionysius against the Syracusans, offered them battle, which was sharply contested, the two sides being equal in strength. In this engagement he had the advantage at first, through his own valour; but when the Syracusans surrounded his galley to box him in, after having done great things in person to disengage himself and seeing no hope of relief, he took with his own hand the life he had so freely and uselessly exposed to the enemy.

Moulay Mohammed, king of Fez, who recently defeated Sebastian, king of Portugal, in the battle so famous for the death of three kings and the passing of that great kingdom to the crown of Castile, was extremely sick when the Portuguese entered his territory in arms. From that day on he grew steadily worse, drawing nearer to his end and foreseeing it. Yet no man ever used his remaining strength more vigorously and bravely than he did on that occasion. He felt too weak to undergo the pomp and ceremony of entering his camp, which in their fashion is magnificent, and so resigned that honour to his brother — but this was all of the general's role that he gave up. Everything else of any real use or necessity he carried out with exactness and glory, in his own person, his body stretched on a couch but his judgment and courage upright and firm to his last breath, and in a sense beyond it. He could have worn out his enemy, who had imprudently advanced into his territory, without striking a blow; and it was a very unfortunate circumstance that, for want of a little life or anyone to substitute in the conduct of the war and the affairs of a troubled state, he was driven to seek a doubtful and bloody victory when he already had a surer, better one in hand. Even so, he managed his lingering illness wonderfully, using it to wear out the enemy and to draw them far from the help of their fleet and the ports they held on the African coast, right up to the last day of his life, which he deliberately reserved for this great battle. He arranged his battalions in a circle, surrounding the Portuguese army on every side, and this circle closing in and drawing tight not only hindered the Portuguese in the fight — which was sharp enough thanks to the valour of the young invading king, since they had to present a front in every direction — but also blocked any flight after the defeat, so that, finding every exit held and shut by the enemy, they were forced to bunch up together again:
"Coacerventurque non solum caede, sed etiam fuga,"
Piled up not only in slaughter but in flight.

and there they were slain in heaps on top of one another, leaving the victor a bloody and complete victory. Dying, he had himself carried hurriedly from place to place wherever the need was greatest, and as he passed along the lines, he encouraged the captains and the soldiers one after another. When a corner of his main battalion was broken, there was no holding him from mounting his horse with his sword in his hand. He did his utmost to break free of those around him and rush into the thick of the battle, while they held him back, some by the bridle, some by his robe, others by his stirrups. This last effort completely drained what little life he had left. They laid him on his bed again, but coming to himself, starting as it were out of a swoon, with all other faculties failing him, to give his people notice that they were to conceal his death — the most necessary order he had left to give, so that his soldiers might not be discouraged by the news — he died with his finger pressed to his lips, the usual sign for silence. Who ever lived so long and so far into death? Who ever died more upright, or more like a man?

The most extreme form of facing death with courage, and the most natural, is to look upon it not only without alarm but without concern, continuing the usual course of life right into it, as Cato did, who occupied himself with his reading and went to sleep with a violent and bloody death in his heart and the weapon in his hand with which he had resolved to dispatch himself.

title: Of posting
paragraphs: I was once not the least skilled at this exercise, which suits men of my build, compact and short, but I have given it up; it shakes us up too much to keep at it for long. I was just now reading that King Cyrus, the better to have news brought to him from every part of his empire, which was enormous, had it tested how far a horse could go in a day without rest, and at those intervals stationed men whose job was to keep horses always ready to mount couriers sent to him. Some say this swift system of posting is equal to the flight of cranes.

Caesar says that Lucius Vibullius Rufus, in great haste to carry intelligence to Pompey, rode night and day, constantly taking fresh horses for greater speed; and Caesar himself, according to Suetonius, travelled a hundred miles a day in a hired coach. He was a furious courier — where rivers blocked his way, he crossed them by swimming, without turning aside to look for a bridge or ford. Tiberius Nero, going to see his brother Drusus, who was sick in Germany, covered two hundred miles in twenty-four hours, with three coaches. In the war between the Romans and King Antiochus, T. Sempronius Gracchus, says Livy:
"Per dispositos equos prope incredibili celeritate ab Amphissa tertio die Pellam pervenit."
["By pre-arranged relays of horses, he, with an almost incredible speed, rode in three days from Amphissa to Pella." — Livy, xxxvii. 7.]
And it appears these were established posts, not horses set up for that one occasion.

Cecina's device for sending news back home was even quicker: he took swallows along with him, and released them toward their nests when he wanted to send word, marking them with some colour to signify his meaning, according to a code he and his people had agreed on beforehand.

At the theatre in Rome, fathers carried pigeons in their bosoms, to which they would tie letters when they wanted to send orders home, and the pigeons were trained to bring back a reply. Decimus Brutus used the same trick when besieged in Modena, and others elsewhere have done the same.

In Peru they posted by means of men, who took the couriers on their shoulders in a kind of litter made for the purpose and ran with such agility that, at full speed, the first runners handed off their load to the second without any pause.

I am told that the Wallachians, the Grand Signior's couriers, perform extraordinary journeys, because they have the right to dismount the first person they meet on the road and give him their own worn-out horses; and that to keep themselves from getting tired they bind a broad sash tightly around their waists. I could never find any benefit in it myself.

title: Of ill means employed to a good end
paragraphs: There is a remarkable relation and correspondence in the universal government of the works of nature, which makes it quite clear that it is neither accidental nor run by several masters. The diseases and conditions of our bodies show up in much the same way in states and governments: kingdoms and republics are founded, flourish, and decay with age as we do. We are subject to a build-up of humours, useless and dangerous — whether of the good ones (for even those the physicians fear; and since we have nothing stable in us, they say that an over-brisk and vigorous state of health must be reduced by art, lest our nature, unable to rest in any fixed condition and having nowhere higher to climb to improve itself, make too sudden and disorderly a retreat — which is why they prescribe purges and bleeding for wrestlers, to take down that overflowing health), or else of bad humours, which is the usual cause of sickness. States are very often sick from the same kind of repletion, and various sorts of purging have commonly been applied. Sometimes a great mass of families is sent out to clear the country, seeking new homes elsewhere and encroaching on others. In this way our ancient Franks came from the deepest part of Germany to seize Gaul and drive out its first inhabitants; in this way the infinite flood of men who came into Italy under Brennus and others was put together; in this way the Goths and Vandals, and also the people who now hold Greece, left their native country to go settle elsewhere with more room. There are scarcely two or three small corners of the world that have not felt the effects of such migrations. The Romans set up their colonies by this means: seeing their city grow immensely populous, they relieved it of the more superfluous people and sent them to inhabit and cultivate lands they had conquered. Sometimes too they kept wars going on purpose against some of their enemies, not only to keep their own men in action, for fear that idleness, the mother of corruption, might bring some worse trouble on them:
"Et patimur longae pacis mala; saevior armis Luxuria incumbit."
["And we suffer the ills of a long peace; luxury is more pernicious than war." — Juvenal, vi. 291.]

but also to serve as a bloodletting for their republic, to vent a little of the overheated energy of their youth, to prune the branches off a stock too thick with wood. It was for this end that they kept up so long a war with Carthage.

In the Treaty of Brétigny, Edward III of England would not include in the general peace he then made with our king the dispute over the Duchy of Brittany, so that he might have somewhere to discharge his soldiers, and so that the huge number of Englishmen he had brought over to serve him here would not flood back into England. This was also one reason our King Philip agreed to send his son John on a foreign expedition: so that he could take with him a great many of the hot young men then in his pay.

There are many today who talk the same way, wishing this heat among us could be discharged in some neighbouring war, for fear that all the diseased humours currently dominant in this body politic of ours may spread further, keep the fever at its peak, and finally cause our total ruin. And in truth a foreign war is far more bearable than a civil one. But I do not believe God will favour so unjust a design as for us to pick a quarrel with others for our own advantage:
"Nil mihi tam valde placeat, Rhamnusia virgo, Quod temere invitis suscipiatur heris."
["Rhamnusian virgin, let nothing ever so greatly please me which is taken without justice from the unwilling owners" — Catullus, lxviii. 77.]

And yet the weakness of our condition often forces us into the necessity of using bad means to a good end. Lycurgus, the most accomplished lawgiver there ever was, virtuous as he was, invented this very unjust practice of forcing the helots, who were their slaves, to be drunk, so that the Spartans, seeing them so lost and drowned in wine, might come to detest the excess of this vice. And yet those were still more to blame who long ago allowed condemned criminals, whatever their manner of death, to be cut up alive by the physicians, to give a true picture of our inward parts and build their art on firmer evidence. For if we must go to extremes, it is more excusable to do it for the health of the soul than of the body, as the Romans trained their people in valour and contempt for danger and death by those furious spectacles of gladiators and fencers, who, having to fight to the death, cut, mangled, and killed one another in front of them:
"Quid vesani aliud sibi vult ars impia ludi, Quid mortes juvenum, quid sanguine pasta voluptas?"
["What other end does the impious art of the gladiators propose to itself, what the slaughter of young men, what pleasure fed with blood." — Prudentius, Contra Symmachum, ii. 643.]
And this custom carried on until the time of the Emperor Theodosius:

"Arripe dilatam tua, dux, in tempora famam, Quodque patris superest, successor laudis habeto Nullus in urbe cadat, cujus sit poena voluptas.... Jam solis contenta feris, infamis arena Nulla cruentatis homicidia ludat in armis."

["Prince, take the honours delayed for thy reign, and be successor to thy fathers; henceforth let none at Rome be slain for sport. Let beasts' blood stain the infamous arena, and no more homicides be there acted." — Prudentius, Contra Symmachum, ii. 643.]

It was, in truth, an astonishing example, and very useful for training the populace, to see every day before their eyes a hundred, two hundred, even a thousand pairs of armed men cut each other to pieces with such steady courage that they were never heard to utter one syllable of weakness or pity, never seen to turn their backs, nor take so much as a single cowardly step to avoid a blow, but rather offered their necks to their opponent's sword and presented themselves to receive the stroke. Many of them, when mortally wounded, would send to ask the spectators whether they were satisfied with their conduct before they lay down to die on the spot. It was not enough for them to fight and die bravely — they had to do it cheerfully too, so that they were hissed and cursed if they showed any hesitation about receiving their death. The young girls themselves egged them on:
"Consurgit ad ictus, Et, quoties victor ferrum jugulo inserit, illa Delicias ait esse suas, pectusque jacentis Virgo modesta jubet converso pollice rumpi."

["The modest virgin is so delighted with the sport, that she applauds the blow, and when the victor bathes his sword in his fellow's throat, she says it is her pleasure, and with turned thumb orders him to rip up the bosom of the prostrate victim." — Prudentius, Contra Symmachum, ii. 617.]

The early Romans only condemned criminals to this use, but later they employed innocent slaves in the work, and even free men who sold themselves for it; and beyond that senators and Roman knights, and women too:
"Nunc caput in mortem vendunt, et funus arena, Atque hostem sibi quisque parat, cum bella quiescunt."
["They sell themselves to death and the circus, and, since the wars are ceased, each for himself a foe prepares." — Manilius, Astron., iv. 225.]
"Hos inter fremitus novosque lusus.... Stat sexus rudis insciusque ferri, Et pugnas capit improbus viriles;"
["Amidst these tumults and new sports, the tender sex, unskilled in arms, immodestly engaged in manly fights." — Statius, Sylv., i. 6, 51.]

I would find this strange and incredible, if we did not see every day in our own wars many thousands of men from other nations, for money, staking their blood and their lives in quarrels that are no concern of theirs.

title: Of the Roman grandeur
paragraphs: I will only say a word or two on this enormous subject, to show the simplicity of those who compare the pitiful greatness of our times with that of Rome. In the seventh book of Cicero's Familiar Letters — and let the grammarians strike out the surname "familiar" if they wish, for it is in truth not very appropriate; and those who, instead of "familiar", have substituted "ad Familiares" can find something to back them up in what Suetonius says in his Life of Caesar, that there was a volume of letters of his "ad Familiares" — there is one addressed to Caesar, then in Gaul, in which Cicero repeats these words from the end of an earlier letter Caesar had sent him: "As for Marcus Furius, whom you have recommended to me, I will make him king of Gaul, and if you want me to promote any other friend of yours, send him to me." It was nothing new for a simple Roman citizen, as Caesar then was, to dispose of kingdoms — for he stripped his kingdom from King Deiotarus to give it to a gentleman of the city of Pergamum, called Mithridates; and those who wrote his Life record several cities sold by him; and Suetonius says he once received from King Ptolemy three million six hundred thousand crowns, which was very like selling him his own kingdom:
"Tot Galatae, tot Pontus, tot Lydia, nummis."
["So much for Galatia, so much for Pontus, so much for Lydia." — Claudius in Eutrop., i. 203.]

Mark Antony said that the greatness of the Roman people was visible not so much in what they took as in what they gave away — and indeed some ages before Antony they had dethroned a king with such astonishing authority that in all of Roman history I have seen nothing that more clearly shows the height of their power. Antiochus held all of Egypt, and was on the point of conquering Cyprus and other appendages of that empire. While he was in the midst of his victories, C. Popilius arrived from the Senate, and at their first meeting refused to take his hand until he had first read his letters. When the king had read them and said he would consider them, Popilius drew a circle around him with his cane and said: "Give me an answer to take back to the Senate before you step out of this circle." Antiochus, astonished at the bluntness of so peremptory an order, paused a moment and then replied: "I will obey the Senate's command." Then Popilius greeted him as a friend of the Roman people. To renounce his claim to so great a monarchy and so successful a course of conquest, from the effect of three lines in writing! He had reason, as he afterwards did, to send word to the Senate by his ambassadors that he had received their order with the same reverence as if it had come from the immortal gods.

All the kingdoms Augustus gained by right of war he either restored to those who had lost them or presented to strangers. And Tacitus, on this subject, speaking of Cogidunus, king of Britain, gives us, with a marvellous touch, an instance of that infinite power: the Romans, he says, had from earliest antiquity been accustomed to leave the kings they had subdued in possession of their kingdoms under their own authority,
"Ut haberent instruments servitutis et reges."
["That they might have even kings to be their slaves." — Livy, xlv. 13.]

It is likely that Suleiman, whom we have seen make a gift of Hungary and other principalities, had this consideration more in mind than the one he was in the habit of giving — that he was sated and overloaded with so many monarchies and so much dominion, won by his own valour and that of his ancestors.

title: Not to counterfeit being sick
paragraphs: There is an epigram in Martial — and one of the good ones, for he has all sorts — where he tells with humour the story of Caelius, who, to avoid having to pay court to certain great men of Rome, to attend their morning levees and follow them about town, pretended to have gout; and the better to colour it, he anointed his legs, had them wrapped in many bandages, and counterfeited perfectly both the gait and the face of a gouty man. In the end, Fortune did him the kindness of making him one for real:
"Quantum curs potest et ars doloris Desiit fingere Caelius podagram."
["How great is the power of counterfeiting pain: Caelius has ceased to feign the gout; he has got it." — Martial, Ep., vii. 39, 8.]

I think I have read somewhere in Appian a similar story, of a man who, to escape the proscriptions of the Roman triumvirs, and the better to hide himself from those who hunted him, had disguised himself and added to the disguise this further invention: he pretended to be one-eyed. But when he had a little more freedom and went to take off the plaster he had worn so long over his eye, he found he had actually lost the sight of it altogether, and that it was completely gone. It may be that the action of sight grew dull from being so long unused, and that the optic power was wholly transferred to the other eye, for we can see plainly enough that the eye we keep shut sends some of its strength to its fellow, which will swell and grow larger; and similarly, inaction, together with the heat of the bandages and plasters, might well have brought some gouty humour upon the counterfeiter in Martial.

Reading in Froissart the vow of a band of young English gentlemen to keep their left eyes bound up until they had arrived in France and performed some notable exploit against us, I have often been tickled by the thought that it might have happened to them as it did to those others, and they might have come back with only one eye apiece to the mistresses for whose sake they had made this ridiculous vow.

Mothers have reason to scold their children for pretending to have only one eye, or to squint, or to limp, or to fake any other personal defect, because, apart from the fact that their bodies at that age are tender and may take on a wrong set, Fortune somehow seems to enjoy taking us at our word — and I have heard several stories of people who became really ill by only feigning to be so. I have always been in the habit, on horseback or on foot, of carrying a stick in my hand, even with a certain elegance about it; many have told me that this affectation will one day be turned into necessity. If so, I will be the first of my family to have gout.

But let us stretch this chapter a little, and add another anecdote about blindness. Pliny reports of a man who, dreaming he was blind, found himself so in the morning, without any earlier weakness in his eyes. The force of imagination might be at work here, as I have said elsewhere, and Pliny seems to think the same; but it is more likely that the inward motions in his body, the cause of which the physicians may find out if they like, were what took away his sight and at the same time gave rise to his dream.

Let us add another story, not improper to the subject, that Seneca tells in one of his letters. "You know," he says to Lucilius, "that Harpaste, my wife's fool, has been left on me as a hereditary charge, for I have a natural aversion to those creatures; and if I want to laugh at a fool, I do not need to look far, I can laugh at myself. This fool has suddenly lost her sight: I tell you a strange but very true thing — she does not know she is blind, but constantly nags her keeper to take her out, because, she says, the house is dark. What we laugh at in her, believe me, happens in each of us: no one knows that he is greedy or grasping; and while the blind call for a guide, we stray of our own accord. I am not ambitious, we say — but a man cannot live otherwise in Rome; I am not extravagant, but the city demands a heavy outlay; it is not my fault that I am hot-tempered; if I have not yet settled on any steady way of life, it is the fault of my youth. Let us not look for our disease outside ourselves; it is in us, planted in our entrails, and the very fact that we do not perceive ourselves to be sick makes us harder to cure. If we do not start early to attend to ourselves, when shall we have provided for so many wounds and ills we are overflowing with? And yet we have a most sweet and charming medicine in philosophy, for with all the rest we feel no pleasure until after the cure: this one pleases and heals at once." That is what Seneca says, and it has carried me away from my subject — but the change is to the good.

title: Of thumbs
paragraphs: Tacitus reports that among certain barbarian kings, their custom for making a binding pledge was to join their right hands close together, interlace their thumbs, and when they had pressed hard enough for the blood to show at the tips, lightly pricked them with some sharp instrument and sucked each other's blood.

Physicians say the thumbs are the master fingers of the hand, and that their Latin name comes from "pollere", to be strong. The Greeks called them "antikheir", as if to say a second hand. And it seems the Latins also sometimes used the word in this sense, for the whole hand:
"Sed nec vocibus excitata blandis, Molli pollici nec rogata, surgit."
["Neither to be excited by soft words or by the thumb." — Mart., xii. 98, 8.]
In Rome it was a sign of favour to press the thumbs down and turn them in:
"Fautor utroque tuum laudabit pollice ludum:"
["Thy patron will applaud thy sport with both thumbs" — Horace.]
and a sign of disfavour to raise them and turn them out:
"Converso pollice vulgi, Quemlibet occidunt populariter."
["The populace, with inverted thumbs, kill all that come before them." — Juvenal, iii. 36]

The Romans exempted from military service everyone maimed in the thumbs, on the ground that they no longer had enough strength to hold a weapon. Augustus confiscated the estate of a Roman knight who had maliciously cut off the thumbs of his two young sons to keep them out of the army; and before him, the Senate, during the Italian War, had sentenced Caius Vatienus to perpetual imprisonment and confiscated all his goods for having deliberately cut off his own left thumb to exempt himself from that campaign. Someone — I have forgotten who — after winning a sea battle, cut off the thumbs of all his beaten enemies to render them unable to fight or handle an oar. The Athenians also had the thumbs of the Aeginetans cut off, to deprive them of their advantage at sea.
In Lacedaemon, schoolmasters used to chastise their pupils by biting their thumbs.

title: Cowardice the mother of cruelty
paragraphs: I have often heard it said that cowardice is the mother of cruelty, and I have found by experience that malicious, inhuman animosity and ferocity usually go hand in hand with a kind of feminine weakness. I have seen the most cruel people apt to cry on trivial occasions. Alexander, the tyrant of Pherae, did not dare watch tragedies in the theatre, for fear his citizens should see him weep at the misfortunes of Hecuba and Andromache — the same man who without pity had so many people murdered every day. Is it not meanness of spirit that makes them so pliable to every extreme? Valour, whose effect is to be exercised only against resistance —
"Nec nisi bellantis gaudet cervice juvenci" —
["Nor delights in killing a bull unless he resists." — Claudius, Ep. ad Hadrianum, v. 39.]

stops when it sees the enemy at its mercy. But pusillanimity, to claim that it too was in the game, not having dared to take part in the first act of danger, takes for itself the second act, of blood and massacre. The murders in victories are usually carried out by the riff-raff and camp-followers of an army; and what causes so many unheard-of cruelties in domestic wars is that this rabble makes war by plunging itself up to the elbows in blood and ripping open a body that lies prostrate at its feet, having no sense of any other kind of valour:
"Et lupus, et turpes instant morientibus ursi, Et quaecunque minor nobilitate fera est:"
["Wolves and the filthy bears, and all the baser beasts, fall upon the dying." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 5, 35.]

Like cowardly dogs that at home worry and tear the skins of wild beasts they dared not come near in the field. What is it in our times that makes our quarrels deadly, so that, where our fathers had several degrees of revenge, we now begin with the last, and at the first meeting nothing is to be said but "kill"? What is this but cowardice?

Everyone can see that there is more bravery and disdain in subduing an enemy than in cutting his throat, in making him yield than in putting him to the sword; besides which, the appetite for revenge is more satisfied and pleased when its only aim is to make itself felt. That is why we do not fall on a beast or a stone when they hurt us, because they are incapable of being aware of our revenge; and to kill a man is to save him from the injury and offence we mean to do him. As Bias cried out to a wicked fellow, "I know that sooner or later you will have your reward, but I am afraid I will not be there to see it"; and pitied the Orchomenians because the penitence of Lyciscus for the treason committed against them came at a time when no one remained alive of those who had been hurt by the offence and whom the pleasure of this penitence might have reached. Revenge is to be pitied when the person on whom it is exercised is robbed of any means of suffering under it; for, as the avenger means to look on and enjoy the pleasure of his revenge, so the person he takes revenge on must be a spectator too, in order to be afflicted and to repent. "He will be sorry for it," we say — and because we have given him a pistol shot through the head, do we imagine he will be sorry? On the contrary, if we look closely, we will see that he pulls a face at us as he falls, and is so far from regret that he does not even reproach us; and we do him the kindest service in life, which is to make him die without feeling it, and quickly. We then have to hide and dodge the officers of justice who hunt us, while he is at rest. Killing is good for preventing an offence to come, not for avenging one that is already past, and is more an act of fear than of bravery, of precaution than of courage, of defence than of attack. It is plain that by killing we lose both the true end of revenge and the care of our reputation; we are afraid that, if he lives, he will do us another injury as great as the first. It is not out of animosity toward him but out of concern for yourself that you get rid of him.

In the kingdom of Narsinga this remedy would be useless to us, where not only soldiers but tradesmen as well end their disputes by the sword. The king never refuses a field to any who want to fight, and if they are persons of quality he looks on himself, rewarding the victor with a chain of gold — for which anyone who pleases may fight with him again, so that, having survived one combat, the victor has signed up for many.

If by means of our courage we thought we could always be masters of our enemies and triumph over them at our pleasure, we would be sorry to see them escape us as they do, by dying. But we want victory more for safety than for honour, and in our quarrels we pursue the result more than the glory.

Asinius Pollio, who, as being a worthy man, was the less to be excused, committed a similar fault when, having written a libel against Plancus, he held it back until Plancus was dead — which is to bite your thumb at a blind man, to insult a deaf one, to wound a man who feels nothing, rather than to risk his retort. And it was also said of him that only goblins wrestle with the dead.

Anyone who waits for the author to die whose writings he intends to challenge — what does he say of himself but that he is weak in attack? It was told to Aristotle that someone had spoken ill of him. "Let him do more," he said; "let him whip me too, provided I am not there."

Our fathers were content to answer an insult with the lie, the lie with a box on the ear, and so on. They were brave enough not to fear their adversaries, alive and provoked; we tremble with fear at the very sight of them on their feet. And the truth of this — does it not show in our admirable practice these days, of going after to the death both the man who has offended us and the man we have offended? It is also a kind of cowardice that has introduced the custom of having seconds, thirds, and fourths in our duels. They used to be duels — now they are skirmishes, scuffles, and battles. Solitude must have been terrifying to those who first invented this practice:
"Quum in se cuique minimum fiduciae esset,"

for in danger any kind of company is naturally consoling. Originally, third persons were called in only to prevent disorder and foul play, and to be witnesses to the outcome of the combat; but now things have gone so far that the witnesses themselves join in. Whoever is invited cannot decently stand by as an idle spectator, on pain of being suspected either of want of affection or of want of courage. Quite apart from the injustice and unworthiness of such a thing — of bringing in another man's strength and valour to defend your honour — I see it as a disadvantage to a brave man who relies on himself alone, to mix his fortune with that of a second. Every man runs danger enough on his own account without taking on the risks of someone else, and has enough to do to trust to his own valour for the defence of his life, without putting something so precious into a third man's hands. For unless it has been expressly agreed in advance to the contrary, it becomes a four-way combat, and if your second is killed, you have two on your hands, with good reason; and as for calling it foul play, it is so, yes — as it is foul play, when fully armed, to attack a man who has only the hilt of a broken sword in his hand, or, while clear and untouched, to attack one who is grievously wounded; but if these are advantages you have gained in the course of fighting, you may use them without reproach. The disparity and inequality are weighed and reckoned only from the condition of the combatants at the start; as for the rest, you must take your chance. Even if alone you had three enemies on you at once, your two companions being killed, you have no more wrong done to you than I would do in a battle by running through a man I saw engaged with one of our own, in just the same kind of advantage. The nature of group fighting is such that, where there is troop against troop — as when our Duke of Orleans challenged Henry, king of England, a hundred against a hundred; three hundred against as many, as the Argives against the Lacedaemonians; three against three, as the Horatii against the Curiatii — the multitude on each side is treated as one single man; the risk is mingled and mixed whenever there is company.

I have a domestic interest in this discussion, for my brother, the Sieur de Matecoulom, was at Rome asked by a gentleman he hardly knew, and who was the defendant challenged by another, to be his second; in this duel he found himself paired with a gentleman much better known to him. (I would dearly like an explanation of these rules of honour that so often crash against, and confound, those of reason.) Having dispatched his man and seeing the two principals still on their feet and unhurt, he ran in to disengage his friend. What less could he have done? Should he have stood still, and, if luck had so ordered it, watched the man he had come to defend killed in front of him? What he had done so far did not help the case; the quarrel was still undecided. The courtesy that you can and certainly ought to show your enemy, when you have brought him to a bad pass and have a great advantage over him, I do not see how you can show it when another man's interest is involved, when you are only there as an assistant and the quarrel is not yours; he could be neither just nor courteous at the cost of the man he was there to serve. For this he was released from the prisons of Italy at the prompt and solemn request of our king. Indiscreet nation! We are not satisfied with letting the world know our vices and follies by report alone; we must go to foreign countries to show in person what fools we are. Put three Frenchmen in the deserts of Libya, and they will not live a month together without fighting; so that you would think this travel was deliberately designed to give foreigners the pleasure of our tragedies — and, for the most part, to such as rejoice and laugh at our miseries. We go to Italy to learn fencing, and practise the art at the cost of our lives before we have learned it; though by the rule of discipline we should put theory before practice. We give ourselves away as beginners:
"Primitae juvenum miserae, bellique futuri Dura rudimenta."
["Wretched the elementary trials of youth, and hard the rudiments of approaching war." — Virgil, Aeneid, xi. 156.]

I know that fencing is an art very useful to its end (in a duel between two princes, cousins-german, in Spain, the elder, says Livy, by his skill and dexterity in arms easily overcame the greater and clumsier strength of the younger), and one whose knowledge, as I know from experience, has given some men courage beyond their natural measure. But this is not properly valour, because it leans on technique and rests on something other than itself. The honour of combat consists in the rivalry of courage, not of skill; and this is why I have known a friend of mine, famous as a great master in this art, in his quarrels choose such weapons as would strip him of the advantage, weapons that depended wholly on luck and steadiness, so that his victory would not be put down more to his skill in fencing than to his valour. When I was young, gentlemen avoided the reputation of being good fencers as something against them, and learned to fence with all possible secrecy, as a craft of cunning that detracted from true and natural valour:

"Non schivar non parar, non ritirarsi, Voglion costor, ne qui destrezza ha parte; Non danno i colpi or finti, or pieni, or scarsi! Toglie l'ira a il furor l'uso de l'arte. Odi le spade orribilmente utarsi A mezzo il ferro; il pie d'orma non parte, Sempre a il pie fermo, a la man sempre in moto; Ne scende taglio in van, ne punta a voto."

["They neither shrank, nor vantage sought of ground, They travers'd not, nor skipt from part to part, Their blows were neither false, nor feigned found: In fight, their rage would let them use no art. Their swords together clash with dreadful sound, Their feet stand fast, and neither stir nor start, They move their hands, steadfast their feet remain. Nor blow nor foin they strook, or thrust in vain." — Tasso, Gierus. Lib., c. 12, st. 55, Fairfax's translation.]

Archery contests, tilting, and barriers — mock versions of warlike fighting — were the exercises of our forefathers. This other exercise is less noble in proportion as it serves only a private end; it teaches us to destroy one another against law and justice, and it always produces very bad effects. It is far more worthy and becoming to train ourselves in things that strengthen rather than weaken our state, things that aim at public safety and common glory. The consul Publius Rutilius was the first to teach his soldiers to handle their arms with skill and to join art with valour — not for the purposes of private quarrel, but for war and the contests of the people of Rome, a popular and civic defence. And besides the example of Caesar, who ordered his men to aim chiefly at the faces of Pompey's soldiers in the battle of Pharsalia, a thousand other commanders have thought to invent new forms of weapons and new ways of striking and defending, as the occasion required.

But just as Philopoemen condemned wrestling, in which he excelled, because the preparations involved in it differed from those that belong to military discipline, to which alone he held that men of honour should give themselves wholly, so it seems to me that this technique to which we accustom our limbs, these twists and motions young men are taught in this new school, are not only useless but actually contrary and harmful to the practice of fighting in battle. Our people also commonly use particular weapons specially designed for the duel, and I have seen it disapproved when a gentleman challenged to fight with rapier and dagger turned up in the equipment of a man-at-arms, or when another took his cloak instead of his dagger. It is worth noting that Laches in Plato, speaking of learning to fence in our manner, says he never knew any great soldier come out of that school, especially among the masters; and indeed, as for them, our own experience says the same. As for the rest, we may at least conclude that they are qualities with no relation or correspondence to each other; and in the education of the children of his republic, Plato bans the art of boxing, introduced by Amycus and Epeius, and that of wrestling, by Antaeus and Cercyon, because they have another end than fitting young men for the service of war, and contribute nothing to it. But I see I have somewhat wandered from my theme.

The Emperor Mauricius, warned by dreams and various omens that a certain Phocas, an obscure soldier, would kill him, asked his son-in-law Philip who this Phocas was, what his nature, qualities, and manners were like; and as soon as Philip, among other things, told him the man was cowardly and timid, the emperor immediately concluded that he was a murderer and cruel. What is it that makes tyrants so bloody? Only the anxiety for their own safety, and that their faint hearts can find them no other means of securing themselves than by wiping out those who might hurt them, even down to women, for fear of a scratch:
"Cuncta ferit, dum cuncta timer."
["He strikes at all who fears all." — Claudius, in Eutrop., i. 182.]

The first cruelties are committed for their own sake; from these springs the fear of a just revenge, which afterwards produces a series of new cruelties, to wipe one another out. Philip, king of Macedon, who had so much to do with the Roman people, harrowed by the horror of so many murders committed by his order, and doubting whether he could keep himself safe from so many families he had mortally injured and offended over the years, resolved to seize all the children of those he had had killed and to dispatch them one after another, day by day, and so secure his own repose.

Fine matter is never out of place wherever you put it, and so I, who care more about the weight and usefulness of what I say than about its order and connection, need not be afraid here to bring in an excellent story, even if it is somewhat off to the side; for when they have their own native beauty and can stand on their own merits, the least pretext will serve to draw them into my discourse.

Among others condemned by Philip had been one Herodicus, prince of Thessaly; after him, Philip had had both his sons-in-law put to death, each leaving a young son behind. Theoxena and Archo were their two widows. Theoxena, though much courted to do so, could not be persuaded to remarry. Archo married Poris, the leading man among the Aenians, and had a great many children by him, whom, when she died, she left at a very tender age. Theoxena, moved by maternal affection for her nephews so as to have them under her own eyes and in her own care, married Poris. Then suddenly came the king's edict. This brave-spirited mother, suspecting Philip's cruelty and afraid of what the soldiers would do to these charming and tender children, was bold enough to declare that she would rather kill them with her own hands than hand them over. Poris, startled by this protest, promised to spirit them away and take them to Athens, to put them in the care of some faithful friends of his. They took advantage of an annual festival held at Aenia in honour of Aeneas, and went there. After appearing by day at the public ceremonies and the banquet, they slipped at night into a vessel set ready for the purpose, to escape by sea. The wind was contrary, and finding themselves in the morning in sight of the land they had left overnight, and being pursued by the port guards, Poris saw what was happening and did all he could to make the sailors strain to outrun the pursuers. But Theoxena, frantic with love and revenge, in keeping with her earlier resolution, prepared weapons and poison and laid them out in front of the children. "Come, my children," she said, "death is now the only means of your defence and freedom, and shall give the gods an opportunity to exercise their holy justice. These sharp swords and these full cups will open you the way to it; take courage, fear nothing. And you, my son, who are the eldest, take this steel in your hand, that you may die the more bravely." The children, with so powerful a counsellor on one side and the enemy at their throats on the other, all snatched eagerly at whatever was nearest to hand and, half dead, were thrown into the sea. Theoxena, proud of having so gloriously provided for the safety of her children, clasped her arms with great affection round her husband's neck. "Let us, my friend," she said, "follow these boys, and share the same tomb." And so, embraced, they threw themselves headlong into the sea, so that the ship was carried back without its owners into the harbour.

Tyrants, in order at once to kill and to make their anger felt, have used their ingenuity to invent the most lingering deaths. They want their enemies dispatched — but not so fast that they will not have time to taste their vengeance. And on this score they are sorely perplexed; for if the torments they inflict are intense, they are short; if long, they are not as painful as they wish; and so they torment themselves over the choice of the greatest cruelty. We have a thousand examples of this in antiquity, and I am not sure that we do not, unawares, retain some traces of that barbarity.

Anything that goes beyond a simple death appears to me sheer cruelty. Our justice cannot expect that the man who is not restrained by the fear of being beheaded or hanged should be any more awed by the imagination of a slow fire, pincers, or the wheel. And meanwhile I do not know whether we are not driving them to despair, for what can be the state of a man's soul as he waits twenty-four hours together to be broken on a wheel, or, in the old way, nailed to a cross? Josephus relates that in the time of the war the Romans waged in Judaea, happening to pass a place where they had crucified some Jews three days before, he recognised three of his friends among them, and obtained the favour of having them taken down; two of them, he says, died, but the third lived a long time afterwards.

Chalcondylas, a writer of good credit, in the records he has left of things that happened in his own time and near at hand, tells us, as the most excessive of torments, of one the Emperor Mohammed often practised: cutting men in two across the diaphragm with a single stroke of a scimitar, so that they died two deaths at once. Both parts, he says, were seen to twitch and struggle for a long time after, in very great torment. I do not think there was much suffering in that movement: the torments that look most dreadful are not always the worst to endure, and I find that those other historians report of him to have been done to the Epirot lords are more horrible and cruel, where they were sentenced to be flayed alive piecemeal, in such a malicious way that they remained fifteen days in that misery.

And these other two: Croesus, having seized a gentleman who was a favourite of his brother Pantaleon, carried him into a fuller's shop, where he had him scratched and combed with the cards and combs of that trade until he died. George Sechel, chief commander of the peasants of Poland, who committed so many atrocities under the name of the Crusade, after being defeated in battle and captured by the Voivode of Transylvania, was bound naked on a rack for three days, exposed to every torment that anyone could devise against him; during which time many other prisoners were kept fasting; in the end, while he was still alive and looking on, they made his beloved brother Lucat, for whom alone he had pleaded, taking all the blame of their crimes upon himself, drink his blood; and they made twenty of his most favoured captains feed on him, tearing his flesh in pieces with their teeth and swallowing the morsels. The rest of his body and his bowels, as soon as he was dead, were boiled, and others of his followers were forced to eat them.

title: All things have their season
paragraphs: Those who compare Cato the Censor with the younger Cato, who killed himself, are comparing two fine natures, much alike. The first earned his reputation in various ways, and stands out for his military exploits and the usefulness of his public service; but the virtue of the younger Cato, quite apart from the fact that it would be blasphemy to set anything beside it in strength, was much purer and unblemished. For who could acquit the Censor of envy and ambition, when he dared to attack the honour of Scipio, a man in goodness and every other excellent quality infinitely beyond him or anyone else of his time?

What they report of him, among other things — that in his extreme old age he took to learning Greek with so eager an appetite, as though to quench a long thirst — does not seem to me to be much in his favour; it is really what we would call lapsing into a second childhood. All things have their season, even good ones, and I may say my Paternoster at the wrong time; as they reproached T. Quintus Flaminius for having been seen praying off to one side while general of an army, during the battle he won.
"Imponit finem sapiens et rebus honestis."
["The wise man limits even honest things." — Juvenal, vi. 444]

Eudemonidas, seeing Xenocrates, very old, still busy with his lectures, said, "When will this man be wise, if he is still learning?" And Philopoemen, to those who praised King Ptolemy for putting his body through arms drill every day, said, "It is not commendable in a king of his age to be exercising in these things; he ought now actually to be using them." The young, say the sages, are to make their preparations, the old to enjoy them; and the greatest fault they see in us is that our desires keep renewing themselves and growing young again — we are always starting to live over.
Our studies and our desires should feel their age; yet here we are with one foot in the grave, and still our appetites and pursuits keep springing up fresh inside us:
"Tu secanda marmora Locas sub ipsum funus, et, sepulcri Immemor, struis domos."
["You against the time of death have marble cut for use, and, forgetful of the tomb, build houses." — Horace, Od., ii. 18, 17.]

The longest of my designs does not stretch beyond a year. My thoughts are now only of finishing; I am ridding myself of every new hope and project, taking my last leave of every place I leave, and every day dispossessing myself of what I have.
"Olim jam nec perit quicquam mihi, nec acquiritur.... plus superest viatici quam viae."

["Henceforward I will neither lose, nor expect to get: I have more wherewith to defray my journey, than I have way to go." (Or): "Hitherto nothing of me has been lost or gained; more remains to pay the way than there is way." — Seneca, Ep., 77. (The sense seems to be that so far he had met his expenses, but that for the future he was likely to have more than he required.)]
"Vixi, et, quem dederat cursum fortuna, peregi."
["I have lived and finished the career Fortune placed before me." — Aeneid, iv. 653.]

Indeed this is the one comfort I find in my old age, that it deadens in me several of the cares and desires that troubled my life: the care of how the world goes, the care of wealth, of grandeur, of knowledge, of health, of myself. There are men who are learning to speak when they should be learning to be silent for good. A man can always study, but he must not always be in school: what a pitiable thing is an old man at his ABCs.
"Diversos diversa juvant; non omnibus annis Omnia conveniunt."
["Various things delight various men; all things are not for all ages." — Gall., Eleg., i. 104.]

If we must study, let us study what fits our present condition, so that we can answer as that man did who, being asked to what end he was studying in his decrepit age, replied, "That I may go out the better, and the more at my ease." Such was the study of the younger Cato, when he felt his end approaching, and which he met with in Plato's discourse on the eternity of the soul — not, as we should think, that he was not long since equipped with every kind of provision for such a departure; for in steadiness, settled will, and instruction he had more than Plato has in all his writings; his knowledge and his courage were, on this point, above philosophy. He applied himself to this study, not for the sake of his death, but as a man whose sleep was never broken by the importance of such a decision, who without choice or change went on with his studies along with the other usual activities of his life. The night he was refused the praetorship he spent in play; the night he was to die he spent in reading. The loss of life or of office was all one to him.

title: Of virtue
paragraphs: I find by experience that there is a great difference between the flights and surges of the soul and a settled, constant habit; and I can quite well see that there is nothing we cannot do, even to outdoing the divinity itself, as a certain man says, since it is more to make oneself impassive by one's own study and effort than to be so by natural condition; and even to join to man's frailty and weakness a god-like resolution and assurance. But these are by fits and starts; and in the lives of those heroes of the past there are sometimes miraculous impulses that seem infinitely to exceed our natural strength, yet they are only impulses. It is hard to believe that these elevated qualities can so thoroughly tincture and soak the soul of a man as to become ordinary in him, almost natural. It happens accidentally even to us, the failures and abortive sketches of men, to launch our souls, when stirred up by other people's words or examples, far beyond their usual reach; but it is a kind of passion that pushes and shakes them and in some way carries them out of themselves. Once this disturbance is over, we see how they imperceptibly droop and slack off, if not down to the very bottom, at least to the point where they are no longer the same — so much so that on every trivial occasion, the loss of a bird, the breaking of a glass, we let ourselves be moved hardly less than one of the common people. I am of the opinion that, except for order, moderation, and constancy, all things are to be done by a man who is altogether imperfect and defective. That is why, the sages say, to judge a man rightly you must mainly look into his ordinary actions, and catch him in his everyday clothes.

Pyrrho, who erected such a charming system of knowledge upon ignorance, tried, like all the others who were genuinely philosophers, to make his life match his doctrine. And because he held that the weakness of human judgment was so extreme as to be incapable of any choice or inclination, and would have it always wavering and suspended, regarding and receiving all things as indifferent, it is said that he always wore the same demeanour and countenance: if he had begun talking, he would finish what he had to say even if the person he was speaking to had walked off; if he was walking, he never stopped for any obstacle in his path, his friends watching to keep him from precipices, collisions with carts, and other such accidents; for to fear or to avoid anything would have gone against his own propositions, which stripped the senses themselves of all power of choice and certainty. Sometimes he submitted to incision and cauterising with such steadiness as never to be seen even to flinch. It is something to bring the soul to these convictions; it is more to put them into effect — and yet not impossible; but to combine them with such perseverance and constancy as to make them habitual, in attempts so remote from common usage, is almost incredible to be done. That was why, being surprised one day at home in a sharp quarrel with his sister, and reproached for breaking his own rules of indifference, he said, "What! Must this scrap of a woman also serve as evidence against my principles?" Another time, when he was seen defending himself against a dog, he said, "It is very hard wholly to put off man; and we must do our best to resist and meet things first by effects, but at least by reason and argument."

About seven or eight years ago, a peasant who is still alive, no more than two leagues from my house, who had long been tormented by his wife's jealousy, came home one day from his work, and as she greeted him with her usual scolding, fell into such a fury that with a sickle still in his hand he cut off then and there all those parts of himself that she was jealous of, and threw them in her face. And it is said that a young gentleman of our nation, lively and amorous, having by his perseverance at last softened the heart of a fair mistress, was enraged when at the point of consummation he found himself unable to perform, and that,
"Nec viriliter Iners senile penis extulit caput."

as soon as he got home he cut off the offending member and sent it to his mistress as a cruel and bloody offering in expiation of his fault. If this had been done out of considered reflection, and on religious grounds, as the priests of Cybele did, what should we say of so high an action?

A few days ago at Bergerac, five leagues from my house, up the river Dordogne, a woman who the night before had been beaten and abused by her husband, a quick-tempered ill-natured fellow, resolved to escape his ill-treatment at the cost of her life. As soon as she was up the next morning, she went, as she usually did, to visit her neighbours, and after letting fall some words to settle her affairs, she took a sister of hers by the hand and led her to the bridge. There, after a sort of jesting goodbye, without any change in her face, she threw herself headlong from the top into the river and was drowned. The most remarkable thing in this is that her resolution had been forming a whole night in her head.

It is quite another matter with the women of India. There it is the custom for men to have many wives, and for the wife who has been most loved to kill herself at her husband's death; so each of them makes it her life's work to win this privilege and gain this advantage over her companions, and the good services they render their husbands aim at no other reward than to be chosen to accompany him in death:

"Ubi mortifero jacta est fax ultima lecto, Uxorum fusis stat pia turba comis Et certamen habent lethi, quae viva sequatur Conjugium: pudor est non licuisse mori. Ardent victrices, et flammae pectora praebent, Imponuntque suis ora perusta viris."

["For when they threw the torch on the funeral bed, the pious wives with hair dishevelled, stand around striving, which, living, shall accompany her spouse; and are ashamed that they may not die; they who are preferred expose their breasts to the flame, and they lay their scorched lips on those of their husbands." — Propertius, iii. 13, 17.]

A certain author of our times reports that he has seen this custom in practice in those Eastern nations: not only the wives bury themselves with their husbands, but the slave-girls he has enjoyed as well, in this fashion. The husband being dead, the widow may, if she wishes (and few do), claim two or three months' grace to put her affairs in order. When the day comes, she mounts on horseback, dressed as finely as on her wedding day, and with a cheerful face says she is going to sleep with her husband, holding a looking-glass in her left hand and an arrow in the other. So escorted in pomp, attended by her relatives and friends and a great crowd of joyful people, she is brought at last to the public place set aside for such spectacles. This is a great square, in the middle of which is a pit full of wood, and next to it a platform with four or five steps, on which she is brought and served with a magnificent feast. After that she falls to dancing and singing, and when she thinks fit gives the order to light the fire. Once this is done, she comes down, and taking the nearest of her husband's relations by the hand, walks with him to a river close by, where she strips herself naked, and having handed her clothes and jewels to her friends, plunges into the water, as if to cleanse herself from her sins. Coming out, she wraps herself in a yellow linen cloth twenty-five ells long and, again giving her hand to her husband's kinsman, returns to the platform, where she gives a speech to the people and commends her children to them, if she has any. Between the pit and the platform a curtain is usually drawn, screening the burning furnace from her sight; some, to show greater courage, forbid this. When she has finished speaking, a woman presents her with a vessel of oil, with which she anoints her head and her whole body, and when she has done, she throws it into the fire, and in an instant flings herself in after. At once the people throw a great quantity of logs and billets on her so that she may not be long in dying, and turn all their joy into mourning. If they are persons of meaner condition, the body of the deceased is carried to the place of burial, and there set sitting, the widow kneeling before him, embracing the dead body; and they remain in this posture while the people build a wall around them, which, as soon as it reaches the woman's shoulders, one of her relations comes from behind and takes hold of her head and twists her neck. As soon as she is dead, the wall is quickly raised and closed up, and there they remain entombed.

There was in this same country something like this among their gymnosophists; for not by anyone else's compulsion nor by the rush of a sudden mood, but as an explicit profession of their order, their custom was, when they had reached a certain age or saw themselves threatened by some illness, to have a funeral pyre raised for them, with a stately bed on top, and after joyfully feasting their friends and acquaintances, to lay themselves down with such resolution that, when the fire was applied, they were not seen to stir hand or foot. In this way one of them, called Calanus, died in the presence of the whole army of Alexander the Great. And he was reckoned neither holy nor happy among them who did not destroy himself like this, sending his soul out purged and purified by the fire, after consuming everything earthly and mortal. This steady premeditation throughout the whole life is what makes the thing astonishing.

Among our other controversies, that of Fate has also slipped in; and to tie things to come, and even our own wills, to a certain and inevitable necessity, we are still resting on this argument from the past: "Since God foresees that all things will fall out as they do, which no doubt he does, then it must follow necessarily that they fall out so" — to which our masters reply: "To see something come to pass, as we do, and as God himself does (for all things being present to him, he sees rather than foresees), is not to compel the event; that is, we see because things fall out, but things do not fall out because we see; events cause knowledge, but knowledge does not cause events. What we see happen, happens; but it might have happened otherwise; and God, in the list of the causes of events which he holds in his foreknowledge, also has the ones we call accidental and voluntary, depending on the freedom he has given to our free will, and he knows that we do wrong because we have willed to."

I have seen many commanders rouse their soldiers with this fatal necessity; for if our time is fixed at a certain hour, neither the enemies' shot nor our own boldness, neither our flight nor our cowardice, can shorten or prolong our life. This is easily said, but see who is so easily persuaded. And if it is true that a strong and lively faith brings actions of its own kind along with it, certainly this faith of ours that we make so much noise about is very faint in this age of ours — unless the contempt it has for works makes it disdain their company. As to this very point, the Sire de Joinville, as credible a witness as you could ask for, tells us of the Bedouins, a nation among the Saracens with whom King St Louis dealt in the Holy Land, that they believed so firmly in their religion that the number of every man's days was set from all eternity by an unalterable decree, that they went naked to war, with nothing but a Turkish sword, and their bodies covered only with a white linen cloth; and that the worst curse they could invent when they were angry was always on their lips: "Cursed be you, like the man who arms himself for fear of death." That is a testimony of faith far beyond ours. Of the same kind too is what was given by two friars of Florence in our fathers' days. Being caught up in a learning controversy, they agreed both of them to go into the fire in the sight of the whole populace, each to verify his own argument, and everything was already prepared and the thing on the point of execution when it was interrupted by an unexpected accident.

A young Turkish lord, having performed a notable exploit in his own person within sight of both armies, that of Murad and that of Hunyadi, on the point of joining battle, was asked by Murad what, in such tender and inexperienced years (for this was his first taste of arms), had inspired him with so brave a courage. He replied that his chief tutor in valour had been a hare. "For one day," he said, "out hunting, I came on a hare in her form, and although I had a brace of excellent greyhounds with me, I thought it would be surest to use my bow, since she sat very fair. I shot at her, and shot all forty arrows that I had in my quiver, not only without hurting her, but without even startling her from her form. At last I slipped my dogs after her, but to no more purpose than the shooting had been. From which I understood that she had been kept safe by her destiny, and that neither arrows nor swords can wound without the leave of fate, which we can neither hasten nor put off." This story may serve, in passing, to show how flexible our reason is to all sorts of images.

A man of advanced years, of name, dignity, and learning, boasted to me that he had been moved to a certain very important change in his faith by a strange and odd inducement, and one in itself so inadequate that I found it much stronger as an argument the other way; he called it a miracle, and so do I, but in a different sense. The Turkish historians say that the conviction those of their nation have stamped into them, about the fated and unalterable allotment of their days, plainly serves to give them great assurance in dangers. And I know a great prince who makes very fortunate use of it, whether he really believes it or only makes it his pretext for risking himself so amazingly. Let us hope Fortune does not get tired too soon of her favour to him.
There has not happened in our memory a more admirable example of resolution than in the two men who conspired against the life of the Prince of Orange.
[The first of these was Jehan de Jaureguy, who wounded the Prince 18th March 1582; the second, by whom the Prince was killed 10th July 1584, was Balthazar Gerard.]

It is amazing how the second, who actually carried it out, could ever have been brought to undertake an attempt in which his predecessor, having tried his utmost, had had such poor success; and by the same method, with the same kind of weapons, to go and attack a lord armed with so recent a lesson in suspicion, powerful in followers and bodily strength, in his own hall, surrounded by his guards, in a city wholly devoted to him. He must have employed a very resolute arm and a courage inflamed by furious passion. A dagger is surer for striking home; but because it requires more motion and more strength of hand than a pistol, the blow is more liable to be parried or blocked. That this man was not running to certain death I do not greatly doubt, because no encouragement anyone could offer him could find any place in a sober mind, and the conduct of his exploit shows plainly enough that he had no shortage of that, any more than of courage. The motives for so powerful a persuasion may be various, for our imagination does as it pleases with itself and with us. The attempt that was made near Orléans was nothing like this; there was more of chance in it than of vigour; the wound was not mortal, if Fortune had not made it so; and to attempt to shoot from horseback, at a great distance, with the rider's body in motion from the motion of the horse, was the deed of a man who would rather miss his shot than miss saving himself. This was clear enough from what followed, for he was so stunned and stupefied by the thought of so great a deed that he completely lost his head, both for finding a way to escape and for governing his tongue. What did he need more than to ride back to his friends across the river? I have done it myself in less danger — and I think it very little risk, however wide the river may be, provided your horse has an easy way in, and you can see an easy landing on the other side according to the current. The other one, when they read out his dreadful sentence, said: "I was prepared for this in advance, and I will make you marvel at my patience."
The Assassins, a nation bordering on Phoenicia,

are reckoned among the Muslims a people of very great devotion and purity of manners. They hold that the surest way to gain Paradise is to kill someone of a different religion, which is why they have often been seen, one or two at a time, and unarmoured, to attack powerful enemies at the price of certain death, without any thought for their own danger. In this way our Raymond, Count of Tripoli, was assassinated (a word derived from their name) in the heart of his own city, during our enterprises of the Holy War; and likewise Conrad, Marquis of Montferrat — the murderers carrying themselves at their execution with great pride and glory at having performed so brave a deed.

title: Of a monstrous child
paragraphs: This story shall stand by itself; I will leave it for physicians to discuss. Two days ago I saw a child whom two men and a nurse, who said they were the father, the uncle, and the aunt, were taking around to earn money by showing it, because it was so strange a creature. In every other respect it was of ordinary shape, could stand on its feet, walk and prattle much like other children of the same age, and so far had taken no other nourishment than the nurse's breasts; what they tried, in my presence, to put into its mouth, it merely chewed a little and spat out again without swallowing; its cry did seem a little odd and peculiar; it was just fourteen months old. Under the breast it was joined to another child, but without a head, and with the spine of the back without movement, the rest entire — one arm was shorter than the other, but had been broken by accident at birth. They were joined breast to breast, as though a smaller child were trying to throw its arms about the neck of a slightly bigger one. The joint and the thickness of the place where they were joined was no more than four fingers, or thereabouts, so that if you pushed the imperfect child upward, you could see the other one's navel below it, the joining being between the chest and the navel. The navel of the imperfect child could not be seen, but all the rest of its belly could; so that everything that was not joined of the imperfect one — arms, buttocks, thighs, and legs — hung dangling from the other and could reach down to mid-leg. The nurse also told us that it urinated through both bodies, and that the limbs of the other body were nourished, had feeling, and were in the same condition as those of the one she was suckling, except that they were shorter and smaller. This double body and several limbs attached to one head might be read as a favourable omen for the king, that he would keep the various parts of our state under the union of his laws; but for fear the event should prove otherwise, it is better to leave it alone, since with things already past there is no need for divination,
"Ut quum facts sunt, tum ad conjecturam aliqui interpretatione revocentur;"
["So as when they are come to pass, they may then by some interpretation be recalled to conjecture" — Cicero, De Divin., ii. 31.]
as it is said of Epimenides that he always prophesied backwards.

I have just seen a herdsman in Médoc, about thirty years old, with no sign of any genital parts; he has three holes through which he constantly passes water; he is bearded, has desire, and seeks contact with women.

Those whom we call monsters are not so to God, who sees in the immensity of his work the infinite forms he has comprehended in it; and it is to be believed that this figure that astonishes us is related to some other figure of the same kind unknown to man. From his all-wisdom nothing proceeds but what is good, common, and regular; but we do not see the order and connection:
"Quod crebro videt, non miratur, etiamsi, cur fiat, nescit. Quod ante non vidit, id, si evenerit, ostentum esse censet."
["What he often sees he does not admire, though he be ignorant how it comes to pass. When a thing happens he never saw before, he thinks that it is a portent." — Cicero, De Divin., ii. 22.]

Whatever falls out contrary to custom we call contrary to nature, but nothing whatsoever is contrary to her. Let this universal and natural reason expel the error and astonishment that novelty brings with it.

title: Of anger
paragraphs: Plutarch is admirable throughout, but especially when he judges human actions. What fine things he says, in his comparison of Lycurgus and Numa, on the subject of our great folly in leaving children to the care and government of their fathers. Most of our civil governments, as Aristotle says, leave each man, like the Cyclopes, to arrange his wives and children according to his own foolish and inconsiderate fancy; the Lacedaemonian and Cretan constitutions are almost the only ones that have committed the education of children to the laws. Who does not see that everything in a state depends on the upbringing of children? And yet they are left to the mercy of parents, however foolish and ill-conditioned they may be, without any kind of supervision.

Among other things, how often, walking through our streets, have I had a good mind to set up a farce to avenge the poor boys I have seen flayed, knocked down, and miserably beaten by some father or mother in their fury, mad with rage. You can see them come out with fire and fury sparkling in their eyes:
"Rabie jecur incendente, feruntur, Praecipites; ut saxa jugis abrupta, quibus mons Subtrahitur, clivoque latus pendente recedit,"
["They are headlong borne with burning fury as great stones torn from the mountains, by which the steep sides are left naked and bare." — Juvenal, Sat., vi. 647.]

(and according to Hippocrates, the most dangerous illnesses are those that disfigure the face), with a roaring and terrifying voice, very often aimed at children only just out of the nursery, who are then crippled and ruined with blows, while our justice takes no notice of it, as if these injuries and dislocations were not being inflicted on members of our commonwealth:
"Gratum est, quod patria; civem populoque dedisti, Si facis, ut patrix sit idoneus, utilis agris, Utilis et bellorum et pacis rebus agendis."
