["It is well when to thy country and the people thou hast given a citizen, provided thou make fit for his country's service; useful to till the earth, useful in affairs of war and peace" — Juvenal, Sat., xiv. 70.]

There is no passion that so much carries men away from their right judgment as anger. No one would hesitate to punish a judge with death who condemned a criminal because of his own bad temper; why then should fathers and schoolmasters be allowed to whip and chastise children in their anger? It is no longer correction, but revenge. Chastisement is to children what medicine is, and would we tolerate a physician who flew into a rage at his patient?

We ourselves, to do the thing properly, should never lay a hand on our servants while we are still angry. While the pulse is racing and we feel ourselves moved, let us put the business off; things will look different to us once we are calm and cool. It is passion that is then in command, passion that speaks, not us. Faults seen through passion look much greater than they really are, as bodies do when seen through a mist. A man who is hungry uses food; but a man who is going to use chastisement should be neither hungry for it nor thirsty. Besides, chastisement that is given with weight and discretion is much better received and more beneficial to the one who suffers it; otherwise he will not think himself justly condemned by a man carried away with anger and fury, and will plead his master's excessive passion, his inflamed face, his unwonted oaths, his agitation and headlong rashness, in his own defence:
"Ora tument ira, nigrescunt sanguine venae, Lumina Gorgoneo saevius igne micant."
["Their faces swell, their veins grow black with rage, and their eyes sparkle with Gorgonian fire." — Ovid, De Art. Amandi, iii. 503.]

Suetonius reports that Caius Rabirius, having been condemned by Caesar, the thing that most prevailed on the people, to whom he had appealed, to decide the case in his favour, was the animosity and vehemence Caesar had shown in passing sentence.

Saying is one thing, doing another; we are to consider the sermon apart from the preacher. They got themselves into a fine business who in our times have tried to shake the truth of our Church by the vices of her ministers; she draws her testimony from elsewhere; it is a foolish way to argue and would throw everything into confusion. A man of good morals may have false opinions, and a wicked man may preach the truth, even though he does not believe it himself. It is, no doubt, a fine harmony when doing and saying go together; and I do not deny that words, when actions follow them, carry greater authority and force — as Eudamidas said, hearing a philosopher talk of military matters: "These things are finely said, but the man who speaks them is not to be believed, for his ears have never been used to the sound of the trumpet." And Cleomenes, hearing an orator declaim on valour, burst out laughing; when the orator was offended at this, he said, "I would do the same if it were a swallow speaking on this subject; but if it were an eagle, I would gladly listen." I notice, I think, in the writings of the ancients, that the man who speaks what he really thinks strikes much closer to home than the man who merely fakes it. Hear Cicero speak of the love of liberty; hear Brutus speak of it: the bare written words of this last man sound as though he would purchase it at the price of his life. Let Cicero, the father of eloquence, treat of contempt for death; let Seneca do the same: the first drawls it out languidly, so that you can see he wants to make you resolve on a thing he is not himself resolved on; he gives you no courage, because he has none himself; the other rouses and fires you. I never read an author, even one writing of virtue and of action, without curiously enquiring what kind of man he was himself; for the Ephors at Sparta, seeing a dissolute fellow propose a sound piece of advice to the people, ordered him to hold his peace, and asked a virtuous man to claim the invention as his own and to put it forward. Plutarch's writings, if they are well understood, sufficiently reveal their author, and so well that I feel I know him into his very soul; and yet I could wish that we had some fuller account of his life. And I have wandered this far from my subject because I am indebted to Aulus Gellius for having left us in writing this story about Plutarch's manners, which brings me back to my theme of anger. A slave of his, a vicious and ill-conditioned fellow, but who had often had the precepts of philosophy ringing in his ears, having for some fault been stripped at Plutarch's command and while being whipped, muttered at first that it was without cause and that he had done nothing to deserve it; but at last falling in good earnest to exclaim against and abuse his master, he reproached him with not being the philosopher he had boasted of being: that he had often heard him say it was indecent to be angry, had even written a book about it, and that having him so cruelly beaten in the height of his rage gave the lie to everything he had written. To which Plutarch calmly and coldly replied: "How now, ruffian, by what do you judge that I am angry? Does my face, my colour, or my voice give any sign that I am moved? I do not think my eyes look fierce, that my face appears troubled, or that my voice is terrifying; am I red, do I foam, does any word escape my lips that I should repent? Do I start? Do I tremble with fury? For those, I tell you, are the true signs of anger." And then, turning to the man who was whipping him, he said, "Go on with your work, while this gentleman and I dispute." That is the story.

Archytas of Tarentum, returning from a war in which he had been general, found everything at his house in great disorder and his lands wholly out of cultivation, through the bad management of his steward, and having had him called in said: "Go — if I were not angry I would soundly drub your sides." Plato likewise, being highly offended with one of his slaves, ordered Speusippus to chastise him, excusing himself from doing it on the ground that he was angry. And Charillus, a Lacedaemonian, to a helot who behaved insolently toward him, said: "By the gods, if I were not angry, I would have you put to death right now."

It is a passion that takes pleasure in itself and flatters itself. How often, when we have been stirred up on a false ground, if the person offending makes a good defence and offers us a just excuse, do we get angry against the truth and innocence itself? On this score I remember a remarkable example from antiquity.

Piso, otherwise a man of very eminent virtue, being angered against a soldier of his because, returning alone from foraging, he could give him no account of where he had left a comrade, took it for granted that he had killed him, and immediately condemned him to death. He had just been put on the gallows when, behold, the wandering comrade arrived — at which the whole army was delighted, and after many embraces between the two friends, the executioner brought the one and the other into Piso's presence, everyone there believing it would be a great pleasure to him too; but it turned out quite otherwise, for through shame and spite, his fury, which had not yet cooled, redoubled, and by a subtlety his passion suddenly suggested to him, he made three guilty men out of having found one innocent and had them all put to death — the first soldier, because sentence had been passed on him; the second, who had lost his way, because he was the cause of his comrade's death; and the executioner, for not having obeyed the order given to him. Anyone who has had to deal with peevish and obstinate women may have experienced what a rage it puts them in to oppose silence and coolness to their fury, and that one disdains to feed their anger. The orator Caelius was wonderfully short-tempered by nature, and to one who supped in his company, a man of gentle and mild conversation, who, so as not to provoke him, approved of and agreed with everything he said, Caelius, unable to bear that his bad mood should waste itself like this without food, said: "For the love of the gods, deny me something, so that we may be two." Women, in the same way, are angry only that others may be angry back, in imitation of the laws of love. Phocion, to a man who interrupted his speech with insulting and very abusive words, made no other reply than silence, giving him full leave and time to vent his spleen; which when he had accordingly done, and the storm had blown over, Phocion went on with his speech where he had left off, without any mention of the interruption. No reply can sting a man like that kind of contempt.

Of the most short-tempered man in France — anger is always a flaw, but more excusable in a soldier, since in that trade it cannot always be avoided — I often say that he is the most patient man I know, and the most discreet in bridling his passions, which rise in him with such violence and fury,

"Magno veluti cum flamma sonore Virgea suggeritur costis undantis ahem, Exsultantque aatu latices, furit intus aquae vis. Fumidus atque alte spumis exuberat amnis, Nec jam se capit unda; volat vapor ater ad auras;"

["When with loud crackling noise, a fire of sticks is applied to the boiling caldron's side, by the heat in frisky bells the liquor dances; within the water rages, and high the smoky fluid in foam overflows. Nor can the wave now contain itself; the black steam flies all abroad." — Aeneid, vii. 462.]

that he has to constrain himself cruelly to moderate it. For my own part, I know no passion which I could with such effort try to cover and conceal; I would not set wisdom at so high a price, and I look not so much at what a man does as at how much it costs him to do no worse.

Another man boasted to me of the steadiness and gentleness of his manner, which is in truth quite remarkable. I replied that it was indeed something, especially in a man of his eminent station, on whom every eye is fixed, to present himself always well-tempered to the world; but that the main thing was to make provision within and for himself, and that in my opinion it was not very good to settle his affairs outwardly well and grate himself within — which I was afraid he was doing in putting on and keeping up this mask and outward appearance.

A man absorbs anger by hiding it, as Diogenes told Demosthenes, who, for fear of being seen in a tavern, drew himself further inside: "The more you draw back, the further in you go." I would rather advise a man to give his servant a box on the ear a little out of season, than to strain his imagination to put on this grave and composed face; and I had rather show my passions than brood over them at my own expense; they grow less by being voiced and shown; and it is far better for their point to wound others outside than to be turned back on ourselves within:
"Omnia vitia in aperto leviora sunt: et tunc perniciosissima, quum simulata sanitate subsident."
["All vices are less dangerous when open to be seen, and then most pernicious when they lurk under a dissembled good nature." — Seneca, Ep. 56]

I tell all those who have authority to be angry in my household, first, to manage their anger and not to spend it on every occasion, for that both diminishes its value and weakens its effect: rash and constant scolding turns into mere habit and is despised; and what you spend on a servant for stealing is not felt, because it is the same thing he has seen you employ a hundred times against him for having badly washed a glass or set a stool out of place. Second, that they should not be angry to no purpose, but make sure that their rebuke actually reaches the person they are offended with; for usually they rail and shout before he comes in, and go on scolding for an age after he is gone:
"Et secum petulans amentia certat:"
["And petulant madness contends with itself." — Claudian in Eutrop., i. 237.]

they attack his shadow and drive the storm in a place where no one is either chastised or concerned, except by the noise of their voice. In quarrels, too, I condemn those who huff and bluster with no enemy in front of them; those rodomontades should be saved for delivery against the offending party:
"Mugitus veluti cum prima in praelia taurus Terrificos ciet, atque irasci in cornua tentat, Arboris obnixus trunco, ventospue lacessit Ictibus, et sparsa ad pugnum proludit arena."

["As when a bull to usher in the fight, makes dreadful bellowings, and whets his horns against the trunk of a tree; with blows he beats the air, and rehearses the fight by scattering the sand." — Aeneid, xii. 103.]

When I am angry, my anger is very sharp but also very short, and as private as I can make it; I lose myself in promptness and violence, but not in confusion; so that I throw out all kinds of injurious words at random and without choice, and never think to direct my language pointedly to where I imagine it would wound deepest, for I usually use no other weapon than my tongue.

My servants get a better deal from me in great matters than in small ones; the small ones take me by surprise; and the trouble is that once you are on the brink, it does not matter who pushed you — you always go to the bottom; the fall urges, drives, and hurries itself on. In great matters this is my comfort, that they are so obvious that everyone expects a reasonable indignation, and then I take pride in disappointing their expectation; against these I fortify and prepare myself; they unsettle my head and threaten to carry me far if I follow them. I can easily hold myself back from entering one of these passions, and am strong enough, when I expect them, to repel their violence, however great the cause; but if a passion once gets hold of me and seizes me, it carries me away, however small the cause. I bargain like this with those who may have to deal with me: when you see me moved first, leave me alone, right or wrong; I will do the same for you. The storm is born only out of a clash of angers, which easily rise from one another, and are not born together. Let each one have his way, and we shall always be at peace. A useful piece of advice, but hard to follow. Sometimes too it happens that I put on a show of anger, the better to govern my household, without any real emotion. As age makes my humours sharper, I study to oppose them, and I will, if I can, manage it so that for the future I may be all the less peevish and hard to please, in proportion as I have more excuse and inclination to be so — though I have until now been counted among those who have the greatest patience.

One more word to wrap up this argument. Aristotle says that anger sometimes serves as a weapon for virtue and valour. That is plausible; nevertheless, those who contradict him pleasantly answer that it is a weapon of a new kind, because we move all other weapons, but this one moves us; our hand does not guide it, it guides our hand; it holds us, we do not hold it.
